result: Enzalutamide is an FDA-approved second-generation antiandrogen for castration-resistant prostate cancer, but responses are often limited in duration. AR mutations are a known mechanism of resistance to antiandrogens.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 establish the clinical context and rationale for the study. C1 is supported by FDA approval and citations (Tran et al., 2009; Scher et al., 2012). C2 reflects clinical observations about limited response duration. C3 is supported by prior literature (Bergerat and Ceraline, 2009) documenting AR mutations as a resistance mechanism.

result: The authors developed a novel reporter-based mutagenesis screening approach using an AR-regulated EGFP reporter to identify AR mutations conferring resistance to enzalutamide. Proof-of-concept validation was performed using the known bicalutamide-resistance mutation AR W741C.
evaluation: Claims C8-C16 describe the methodological approach and validation. The EGFP reporter system (C13) is supported by Figure 1A and prior work (Chapel-Fernandes et al., 2006). Proof-of-concept with AR W741C (C14-C16) is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1, demonstrating enrichment of the known mutation after bicalutamide selection. The rationale is well-supported by citations (C8-C12).

result: A reporter-based mutagenesis screen identified the novel AR F876L mutation, which converts enzalutamide into an AR agonist. After five rounds of enzalutamide selection and FACS sorting, cells with durable EGFP expression were enriched, and the F876L mutation was identified as the dominant mutation in two of three replicates.
evaluation: Claims C4, C17-C22 describe the primary discovery. The screen methodology is supported by Figure 1A-B showing progressive enrichment of EGFP-positive cells. The identification of F876L is supported by Sanger sequencing (Figure 1C) and enrichment data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). The agonist activity is confirmed by EGFP induction (C18, Figure 1B), endogenous target gene expression (C19, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and AR-dependence via siRNA knockdown (C20, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).

result: AR F876L converts enzalutamide into an agonist, inducing AR transcriptional activity, nuclear localization, chromatin recruitment, and target gene expression. Enzalutamide binds with higher affinity to AR F876L than wild-type AR.
evaluation: Claims C23-C29 characterize the molecular pharmacology of AR F876L. Dose-dependent EGFP induction is shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 (C23). Luciferase induction (~50-fold) is shown in Figure 2B (C24), with comparable effects to known mutations T877A and W741C (C25). Nuclear localization (C26) and chromatin recruitment (C27) are supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B. Target gene expression changes are shown in Figure 2C (C28). Higher binding affinity is demonstrated by competition assay in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 (C29).

result: The F876L mutation similarly converts ARN-509, a structurally related antiandrogen sharing the bisaryl-thiohydantoin core, into an AR agonist.
evaluation: Claim C30 extends the finding to ARN-509. This is supported by Figure 2B showing luciferase induction, and Figure 2—figure supplements 4 and 5 showing EGFP induction and target gene expression. The structural similarity is noted and the pharmacological effect is consistent with enzalutamide.

result: Ectopic expression of AR F876L rescues growth inhibition by enzalutamide in multiple prostate cancer cell lines (VCaP, CWR22Pc) in vitro and in vivo. In xenograft models, AR F876L tumors grew rapidly despite enzalutamide treatment, while wild-type AR tumors were inhibited.
evaluation: Claims C5, C31-C35 demonstrate functional resistance. VCaP growth rescue is shown in Figure 2D (C31) and Figure 2E (C32) in both full serum and androgen-depleted conditions. CWR22Pc results are shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6A,B (C33). In vivo xenograft data (Figure 2F) show that AR F876L tumors grow despite enzalutamide treatment (C34-C35), while wild-type AR tumors are inhibited. These data collectively support that AR F876L confers functional resistance.

result: The F876L mutation spontaneously emerges in prostate cancer models after prolonged treatment with enzalutamide or ARN-509. In vitro, >50% of CWR22Pc cells expressed F876L after enzalutamide treatment. In vivo, F876L was detected in multiple enzalutamide- and ARN-509-resistant xenograft tumors, with one tumor showing 71% F876L frequency.
evaluation: Claims C36-C39 demonstrate spontaneous emergence of resistance. In vitro data (Table 1) show 52% F876L in CWR22Pc cells after enzalutamide treatment (C36) and 1.3% after ARN-509 treatment (C37). In vivo xenograft data (Tables 1 and 2) show F876L in 3/8 enzalutamide-treated and 3/14 ARN-509-treated tumors (C38), with frequencies ranging from ~1-2% to 71% (C39). Deep sequencing provides quantitative support. The F876I variant was also detected (C39).

result: Structure-activity relationship studies show that conservative F876Y substitution does not alter enzalutamide/ARN-509 pharmacology, while aliphatic substitutions (F876I, F876L) confer agonism.
evaluation: Claims C40-C41 describe SAR at position 876. Figure 2—figure supplement 7 shows luciferase assays demonstrating that F876Y does not confer agonism (C40), while F876I does (C41). This supports the importance of aliphatic character at position 876 for agonist conversion. The F876I variant was also found in resistant xenografts (C39), providing biological validation.

result: Bicalutamide does not induce AR F876L transcriptional activity and retains weak antagonist activity at low doses, but loses potency at higher concentrations. Given that AR overexpression is common in CRPC and confers partial agonism to bicalutamide, bicalutamide is not a viable treatment option for patients with AR F876L-mediated enzalutamide resistance.
evaluation: Claims C42-C48 address bicalutamide as a potential alternative. C42 is supported by Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 7 showing no induction. C44 is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 8 showing dose-dependent loss of potency. C45 is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 6A showing minimal growth inhibition. C46-C47 cite prior literature (Linja et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2004). The conclusion (C48) is a reasonable inference, though it relies on the assumption that AR overexpression is present, which is not directly tested in this context.

result: Molecular dynamics simulations suggest that enzalutamide and ARN-509 bind differently than bicalutamide, with the thiohydantoin B-ring forcing the C-ring into an 'H11 pocket' rather than the 'H12 pocket' occupied by bicalutamide. This causes conformational rearrangements in H11 and H12 that prevent H12 from adopting an agonist conformation in wild-type AR. The F876L mutation allows H12 to reposition into a more agonist-like conformation by reducing unfavorable interactions with the C-ring.
evaluation: Claims C49-C63 describe MD simulation results. The structural template (2AXA) is appropriate (C50-C51). The simulations show distinct binding modes (C52-C54, Figure 3B-C) and differential H12 positioning (C55-C60, Figure 3D-E). RMSD measurements (C56-C59) quantify these differences. However, MD simulations are computational predictions that require experimental validation. No crystal structure of AR/enzalutamide complex exists to validate the binding mode. The simulations are internally consistent and provide a plausible mechanism, but the lack of experimental structural validation limits confidence. The consistency with pharmacological data (C63) provides indirect support.

result: MD simulations predict that the substituent at position 4 of the B-ring (gem-dimethyl on enzalutamide, spirocyclobutyl on ARN-509) lies near H12 in the mutant receptor, with the bulkier spirocyclobutyl causing greater H12 displacement in wild-type AR.
evaluation: Claims C64-C65 describe additional MD simulation insights (Figure 3D-E, Figure 4A). These predictions are consistent with the overall model but remain computational predictions without direct experimental validation. The subsequent chemical synthesis and testing (C66-C77) provide indirect validation of these predictions.

result: Based on MD simulation predictions, a series of analogues (DR100-103) with incrementally larger spirocycles on the B-ring were synthesized. DR100-102 behaved as agonists for AR F876L, while (±)-DR103 potently inhibited AR F876L and was more potent against AR F876L than wild-type AR.
evaluation: Claims C66-C70 describe rational drug design based on MD simulations. The synthesis is described in Methods (C66). EGFP reporter assays (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B) show that DR100-103 inhibit AR WT (C67), while DR100-102 are agonists for AR F876L (C68). (±)-DR103 inhibits AR F876L (C69, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2) and is more potent against F876L than WT (C70, Figure 4—figure supplement 3). These data validate the MD simulation predictions and demonstrate successful structure-based drug design.

result: Structure-activity relationship studies of the D-ring position and substitution pattern show that gem-dimethyl placement at position 4 (DR104) confers agonism, while placement at positions 3 and 5 (DR105) or transplantation onto ARN-509 scaffold (DR106) confers antagonism. Removal of the D-ring (DR107) results in agonism for both wild-type and mutant AR.
evaluation: Claims C71-C74 describe detailed SAR studies. Figure 4—figure supplement 1C shows that DR104 (position 4) is an agonist for F876L but antagonist for WT (C71), DR105 (positions 3 and 5) inhibits both (C72), and DR107 (no D-ring) is an agonist for both (C74). Figure 4—figure supplement 1B shows DR106 inhibits F876L (C73). These data demonstrate the critical importance of D-ring position and size for antagonist activity against AR F876L.

result: Three novel compounds (including DR103) effectively antagonize AR F876L and suppress growth of prostate cancer cells resistant to enzalutamide. (±)-DR103 inhibits growth of cell lines expressing both wild-type and mutant AR, while the agonist analogue DR101 does not. The antiproliferative effect is AR-specific, as DR103 does not affect AR-null DU145 cells.
evaluation: Claims C7, C75-C77 demonstrate functional activity of the designed compounds. Growth inhibition by (±)-DR103 is shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4 for both WT and F876L-expressing cells (C75). DR101 (agonist) does not inhibit growth (C76, Figure 4B). Specificity is demonstrated by lack of effect on AR-null DU145 cells (C77, Figure 4—figure supplement 6). Western blots (Figure 4—figure supplement 5) show inhibition of AR signaling. These data support that the designed compounds overcome F876L-mediated resistance.

result: MD simulations suggest that (S)-DR103 prevents H12 from adopting an agonist conformation in both wild-type and mutant AR by directly displacing H12 through occupation of the H12 pocket, rather than by regaining interactions at the F876L mutation site. The two enantiomers may cause different levels of antagonism.
evaluation: Claims C78-C84 describe MD simulations for DR103 enantiomers. Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 7 show that (S)-DR103 causes H12 dislocation in both WT and F876L (C78). Figure 4—figure supplement 8 shows occupation of the H12 pocket (C80) but similar binding in the H11 pocket (C81), suggesting a different mechanism than simply restoring F876 interactions (C82). (R)-DR103 shows less H12 dislocation (C83), suggesting enantiomer-specific effects (C84). However, these are computational predictions. The experiments used racemic (±)-DR103, so enantiomer-specific activity was not directly tested. The simulations provide a plausible mechanism but require experimental validation.

result: Understanding drug resistance mechanisms is crucial for developing strategies to overcome resistance. AR mutations cause clinical resistance to antiandrogens, and the F876L mutation was recovered spontaneously from enzalutamide-treated models, demonstrating that prostate cancer can acquire gain-of-function mutations rather than simple loss-of-binding mutations.
evaluation: Claims C85-C89 provide discussion context. C85 is supported by prior work with kinase inhibitors and antivirals (Shah et al., 2004; Glickman and Sawyers, 2012). C86 is supported by prior literature (Veldscholte et al., 1990; Haapala et al., 2001). C88 is supported by the data in Tables 1 and 2 showing spontaneous emergence. C89 is a reasonable interpretation emphasizing the gain-of-function nature of the resistance mechanism.

result: The MD simulations, informed by prior structural studies of steroid receptors, provide a mechanistic explanation for how F876L converts enzalutamide into an agonist. The simulations successfully predicted compounds that restore antagonism, demonstrating the value of structure-based drug design. The discovery of F876L was essential for identifying the importance of the D-ring, which would have been difficult to identify through conventional screening.
evaluation: Claims C90-C96 discuss the implications of the structural modeling. C90 cites prior work on progesterone and estrogen receptors (Benhamou et al., 1992; Shiau et al., 1998). C91 summarizes the MD simulation mechanism. C92 notes that the predicted compounds (D-ring series) effectively antagonized AR F876L, which is supported by the experimental data (C66-C77). C93-C95 argue that the mutation-driven approach was essential for discovering the D-ring SAR, which is a reasonable interpretation given the subtle structural differences. C96 proposes that MD simulations could guide future drug discovery, which is a reasonable extrapolation pending crystal structure validation.

result: Despite ~50% of patients failing to respond to enzalutamide, the bisaryl-thiohydantoin chemotype remains important. The structural model provides a tool to refine this chemotype into improved drug candidates. Discovery of AR F876L may facilitate crystallographic studies of the enzalutamide/AR complex.
evaluation: Claims C97-C99 discuss future directions. C97 provides clinical context. C98 is a reasonable interpretation of the value of the structural model, supported by the successful design of DR103. C99 is speculative but reasonable, as the F876L mutation stabilizes an agonist conformation that may be more amenable to crystallization.

result: Prior experience with dasatinib-resistant BCR-ABL mutations suggests that preclinically identified resistance mutations can emerge clinically within 2 years. Routine tumor rebiopsy in CRPC is challenging due to osteoblastic bone lesions, but blood-based assays for AR mutation detection may be a viable alternative based on success in other cancers.
evaluation: Claims C100-C102 discuss clinical implications. C100 is supported by prior work (Burgess et al., 2005; Shah et al., 2007) showing that preclinical resistance mutations can predict clinical resistance. C101 describes a known clinical challenge. C102 proposes blood-based assays as an alternative, citing success in other cancers (Diehl et al., 2008; Leary et al., 2012). These are reasonable proposals for future clinical application.
